**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

There’s something about the number one thousand that feels like a threshold—like standing at the edge of a cliff where the wind is just loud enough to drown out your thoughts. A thousand words. That’s roughly two double-spaced pages in a word processor, or about four single-spaced pages in a manuscript. It’s a short story’s worth of space, a poem’s breath, a novel’s whisper. And yet, when you sit down to write it, the blank page yawns back at you like an abyss.

I wonder if the number itself is arbitrary. Why not 999? Or 1,001? Maybe it’s because 1,000 is round, like a zero with a little more weight to it. Like a milestone, even if it’s just a made-up one. We love milestones. We love counting things—steps, calories, likes, days since the last argument. We love the illusion of progress, the way a number can make us feel like we’re moving forward, even when we’re standing still.

But what if I told you that a thousand words is nothing? That it’s the equivalent of a few minutes of speech, the length of a grocery list, the time it takes to microwave popcorn? What if I told you that in the grand scheme of things, a thousand words is less than a drop in the ocean of human expression? Would that make it feel smaller? Or would it free you from the pressure of it?

I think about the first time I wrote a thousand words in a single sitting. It was a school assignment, a short story about a girl who found a door in her closet that led to a world where time moved backward. I remember the way my fingers ached, the way my back stiffened, the way my eyes burned from staring at the screen. I remember the pride I felt when I hit the word count, like I’d just run a marathon. But now, looking back, I wonder if the story was any good. Did it matter? The words were there. The count was met. That was enough.

There’s a kind of tyranny in word counts. They’re the silent judges of writing, the invisible hands that decide whether your work is "enough." Editors demand them. Teachers enforce them. Even in casual writing, like this, the idea of a thousand words looms. It’s a challenge, a game, a test. Can you fill the space? Can you make it mean something?

But what if the words don’t come? What if you sit there, staring at the cursor, and it blinks back at you like a taunt? *You have 1,000 words to write. Where are they?* Sometimes, the pressure is enough to make the words disappear entirely. You overthink. You second-guess. You delete sentences before they’re even finished. And then, before you know it, the blank page wins again.

I’ve been there. I’ve stared at a thousand-word requirement and felt the weight of it like a stone on my chest. I’ve written paragraphs that felt hollow, sentences that sounded forced, just to meet the count. And then I’ve read them back and wondered, *Did I just waste a thousand words?* Because isn’t that the real fear? Not that you won’t write enough, but that you’ll write *too much*—that you’ll fill the space with noise instead of meaning.

But maybe that’s the point. Maybe the thousand words aren’t about the destination. Maybe they’re about the journey—the stumbling, the erasing, the starting over. Maybe the real magic happens in the mess, in the words that don’t quite fit, in the sentences that surprise you. Maybe the count is just a way to trick yourself into starting, into letting the words flow even when they feel meaningless.

I think about the writers who churn out thousands of words a day, who treat writing like a factory assembly line. They’re not wrong. There’s something to be said for discipline, for showing up even when the muse is silent. But there’s also something to be said for the words that come unbidden, the ones that spill out when you’re not trying to meet a quota. Those are the words that feel alive.

So here I am, with my thousand words stretching out before me like an uncharted road. I could write about anything—a memory, a dream, a half-formed idea. I could write about the way the light looks through my window right now, golden and slanted, like it’s holding its breath. I could write about the fear of not having enough to say. I could write about the way numbers feel like cages sometimes.

Or I could just write. Not because I have to, not because someone is counting, but because the words are there, waiting, and if I don’t let them out, they’ll just keep bouncing around in my head like restless ghosts.

So here goes.

The first word is always the hardest. It’s the crack in the dam, the first drop of rain. Once it’s out, the rest follow, sometimes in a rush, sometimes in fits and starts. But they come. They always do.

And maybe that’s the secret. Not to worry about the count. Not to worry about whether the words are good or bad or enough. Just to write them. Just to let them out. Because in the end, a thousand words is just a number. What matters is the act of creation—the stubborn refusal to let the blank page win.

So I’ll keep writing. Even when it’s hard. Even when it feels meaningless. Because somewhere in these thousand words, there might be a sentence that surprises me. A phrase that makes me pause. A thought that lingers.

And if not? Well, at least I tried.

That’s what matters.
